q: There's an index on `(last_name, first_name)`. Can a query `WHERE first_name = 'Ann'` seek through it efficiently?
options: No: first_name isn't the leading column
Only if the table is small
explain: The index is sorted by last_name first, so all 'Ann's are scattered across it. At best the database scans the whole index (or a skip scan in PostgreSQL 18 / MySQL 8.0.13+ helps when last_name has few distinct values).

q: Users log in with any letter case. There's an index on `email`. Why is `WHERE lower(email) = ?` slow, and what's the fix?
options: The index stores email, not lower(email); create an expression index on lower(email)
lower() is slow; do it in Java
Add an index on email DESC
explain: An expression index `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` matches the predicate exactly. Alternatives: store a normalized column, or use the citext type.

q: Which predicate can a plain B-tree index on `name` NOT serve?
explain: A leading wildcard means no known prefix to seek to. In PostgreSQL a trigram GIN index (`pg_trgm`) handles `LIKE '%son%'`.

q: Which index best serves `WHERE status = ? AND created_at > ?`?
options: Two separate indexes are always better
explain: Equality first, range last: the seek goes to `status = X` and then reads one contiguous range of created_at. With created_at first, status could only be filtered, not used for the seek.

q: What is an index-only scan?
options: The query is answered from the index alone, without reading table rows
A scan that reads only the index root
A full scan of all indexes
explain: It needs every referenced column in the index (keys or INCLUDE columns). In PostgreSQL it also depends on the visibility map being up to date.

q: In InnoDB, what does a secondary index entry point to?
options: The primary key value of the row
The page number of the row
explain: So a secondary lookup goes through the secondary index, then through the clustered PK index. That's also why wide PKs make all secondary indexes larger.

q: Why are random UUIDv4 primary keys a problem for InnoDB (and B-trees in general)?
options: Inserts land at random positions: page splits, fragmentation, poor cache locality
They make SELECT by primary key O(n)
explain: Sequential keys append at the right edge of the tree, so the hot pages stay in memory. UUIDv7 keeps the uniqueness of UUIDs with time ordering.

q: A `gender` column has 2 values evenly distributed, and it has an index. Why does the planner ignore it?
options: Low selectivity: reading half the table through an index costs more than a sequential scan
Indexes don't work on text columns
The planner never uses indexes on columns with NULLs
explain: Random page reads for 50% of the rows are slower than one sequential pass. Such an index mostly just slows down writes.

q: Which PostgreSQL index type fits `WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red"}'` on a jsonb column?
explain: GIN indexes each key/value inside the document, which is what containment needs. A B-tree compares whole values only.

q: A 2-billion-row append-only events table is queried by time ranges. You want the smallest possible index. Which type?
explain: BRIN stores min/max per block range, kilobytes instead of gigabytes. It works because rows are physically ordered by time; random order would make it useless.

q: 98% of orders are COMPLETED, and queries only look at the few ACTIVE ones. What's the best index?
options: A partial index: CREATE INDEX ... ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
No index: use a materialized view
explain: A partial index covers only the rows that matter: tiny, always cached, cheap to maintain. The query's WHERE must imply the index predicate.

q: What's the main cost of having many indexes on a write-heavy table?
options: Slower inserts, updates and deletes, plus extra disk, memory and vacuum work
Nothing: indexes are free once created
explain: Each index is updated on every insert and delete. In PostgreSQL extra indexes also prevent HOT updates when an indexed column changes.

q: How do you add an index to a large production PostgreSQL table without blocking writes?
options: LOCK TABLE ... IN SHARE MODE first
explain: A plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes for the whole build. CONCURRENTLY takes longer and can't run inside a transaction block; if it fails it leaves an INVALID index to drop.

q: Which queries can a PostgreSQL hash index serve?
explain: Hashes have no order. Hash indexes are WAL-logged and crash-safe since PostgreSQL 10, but a B-tree is usually just as good.

q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows `rows=10` estimated and `rows=1000000` actual at a scan. What's the likely cause and first fix?
options: Stale or insufficient statistics; run ANALYZE (maybe raise the statistics target)
explain: Bad estimates lead to bad plans (nested loops over a million rows). For correlated columns, extended statistics (`CREATE STATISTICS`) help.

q: With an index on `(a, b)`, why is `WHERE a = 5 ORDER BY b LIMIT 10` fast?
options: Rows come out of the index already sorted by b, so it reads just 10 entries
The index is used only for the filter, and the sort is in memory
explain: No sort node at all: the scan stops after 10 rows. With only an index on `a`, all matching rows would be fetched and sorted.

q: How can PostgreSQL use two separate indexes on a and b for `WHERE a = 1 OR b = 2`?
options: A BitmapOr of two bitmap index scans
It can't; it always does a seq scan
It uses only the first index
explain: Each index produces a bitmap of matching pages, the bitmaps are OR-ed, and the heap is read in page order. Rewriting as UNION is another option.

q: MySQL: `phone` is VARCHAR with an index. Why can `WHERE phone = 5551234` (a number) ignore the index?
options: The column is converted to a number for every row, so the index can't be used
Numbers can't be compared with strings
explain: A type mismatch forces a conversion on the column side. Always bind parameters with the column's type (watch JDBC setters and ORMs).

q: How deep is a typical B-tree index on a 100-million-row table?
explain: With a few hundred keys per 8 KB page, each level multiplies capacity by hundreds. The upper levels are almost always in memory.

q: How do you find indexes that are never used in PostgreSQL?
options: Indexes are dropped automatically when unused
explain: Check over a long period and on all replicas (reads may go there), and keep indexes that back unique or primary key constraints.

q: What is a HOT update in PostgreSQL?
options: An update that writes the new row version on the same page and touches no index
An update holding a hot lock
An update to a cached row
explain: Possible when no indexed column changes and the page has free space (a lower fillfactor helps). It saves index writes and bloat.

q: PostgreSQL: `order_items.order_id` references `orders.id` but has no index. What suffers?
options: Joins from orders to items and deleting orders (each delete scans order_items)
Nothing: PostgreSQL indexes foreign keys automatically
explain: PostgreSQL indexes the referenced side (it must be unique) but not the referencing column. Deleting a parent row has to check the children, a full scan without an index.

q: Why can an Index Only Scan in PostgreSQL still read table pages?
options: Pages not marked all-visible in the visibility map must be checked in the heap
Index-only scans always read the table
The index stores only half the columns
explain: The index doesn't hold visibility (MVCC) information. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows `Heap Fetches`; VACUUM keeps the visibility map current.

q: Which of these is enforced by an index in PostgreSQL?
explain: UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY constraints create unique B-tree indexes. Exclusion constraints use GiST (or other) indexes.
